Keywords: branch create switch checkout -b new feature develop
Description: Create a new branch and switch to it in one step. Modern Git uses git switch -c; older git uses git checkout -b. Both work — switch -c is clearer.
When to Use: Starting work on a new feature, bug fix, or experiment
Command Example:
# Modern (Git 2.23+)
git switch -c feature/add-cors-middleware

# Classic
git checkout -b feature/add-cors-middleware

# From a specific starting point
git switch -c hotfix/login-bug origin/main
Gotchas: Always branch from the correct base (main vs develop). Running git switch -c from a partially-merged branch creates messy history.

Keywords: branch name convention prefix feature bugfix hotfix release slash slash description
Description: Use structured prefixes for branch names so intent is clear at a glance: feature/ bugfix/ hotfix/ release/ chore/. Include ticket numbers when available.
When to Use: Whenever creating a new branch in a team setting
Command Example:
feature/GH-123-add-cors-middleware
bugfix/GH-456-fix-miners-semaphore
hotfix/GH-789-login-crash
release/v2.1.0
chore/update-dependencies
docs/improve-readme
Gotchas: Avoid spaces and uppercase — they cause problems in URLs and some shells. Maximum 50 chars is a good guideline. Avoid generic names like fix or update.

Keywords: delete branch -d -D merged dangling local remote
Description: Delete a local branch with -d (safe — fails if unmerged) or -D (force). Delete a remote branch with git push origin --delete.
When to Use: After a feature branch is merged and no longer needed
Command Example:
# Delete local branch (safe — fails if not merged)
git branch -d feature/add-cors-middleware

# Force delete unmerged branch
git branch -D feature/experiment-abandoned

# Delete remote branch
git push origin --delete feature/add-cors-middleware

# Prune stale remote-tracking refs
git fetch --prune
Gotchas: -D force-deletes even unmerged branches — you will lose those commits unless they are reachable from another ref. Always double-check before force deleting.

Keywords: list branch ls remote all verbose tracking
Description: List local and remote branches. Use -a for all branches -r for remote-only -vv to show tracking information and last commit.
When to Use: Before creating a branch (check if it already exists) or to audit stale branches
Command Example:
# List local branches
git branch

# All branches (local + remote)
git branch -a

# Verbose: show tracking and last commit
git branch -vv

# List merged branches (safe to delete)
git branch --merged main
Gotchas: Remote-tracking refs (remotes/origin/...) are local cache copies — they update on fetch/pull. git branch -a shows them but they may be stale.

Keywords: rename move branch -m current new local remote update
Description: Rename a local branch with git branch -m. Then update the remote by pushing with the new name and deleting the old remote branch.
When to Use: When a branch name has a typo or its scope changed
Command Example:
# Rename the current branch
git branch -m new-branch-name

# Rename a different branch
git branch -m old-name new-name

# Push new name and delete old on remote
git push origin HEAD
git push origin --delete old-name
Gotchas: GitHub/GitLab may have the old branch name in PR titles or protection rules — update those manually after renaming.

Keywords: protect main branch rules force push restrictions review required CI status
Description: Configure branch protection rules on GitHub/GitLab to prevent force-pushes
Command Example: and require CI status checks before merging.
Gotchas: For main develop and release branches in team projects — prevent accidental damage
Docs URL:
# GitHub: Settings > Branches > Add rule
# Protect main with:
# - Require pull request reviews (1+ approvals)
# - Require status checks (CI must pass)
# - Restrict who can push

# Locally: git hooks can help enforce (see hooks domain)
git config branch.main.rebase true
column8: Branch protection is server-side (GitHub/GitLab config). Git hooks can help locally but are not enforced server-side unless used with a hook server.

Keywords: orphan branch gh-pages docs unrelated history new root detached
Description: Create a branch with no parent commits — a completely fresh history tree. Used for GitHub Pages or storing unrelated artifacts alongside code.
When to Use: Creating a GitHub Pages branch, storing documentation, or starting a clean history
Command Example:
# Create a completely clean branch
git switch --orphan gh-pages

# Add files with no prior history
echo 'hello' > index.html
git add .
git commit -m 'Initial gh-pages commit'
Gotchas: Orphan branches share no history with other branches. Merging them back is not straightforward — use with intent. Run git rm -rf . first to clear the working tree.

Keywords: tracking remote upstream set-upstream -u origin fetch
Description: Set a local branch to track a remote branch so git pull and git push work without specifying remote/branch names each time.
When to Use: After cloning a repo, or when you pushed a branch for the first time
Command Example:
# Push and set tracking in one command
git push -u origin feature/my-branch

# Set tracking on an existing branch
git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/feature/my-branch

# Check tracking info
git branch -vv
Gotchas: If tracking is wrong git pull will merge the wrong branch. Always verify with git branch -vv. Remove tracking with git branch --unset-upstream.
